name: Mbéré
parler: Mbéré; Fulfulde as the language of use
overview: The first occupants of the department that bears their name, the Mbéré live in small numbers among the Bororo and the Fulani, whose language they mostly speak. Strongly Islamised, they are renowned as masters of honey and as healers; farming, goat and sheep rearing and pottery complete their activities.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Minority group, relatively isolated, in contact with the Bororo and the Fulani; Fulfulde is mainly spoken there.
Mbéré is also spoken in the East (Bertoua, Garoua-Boulaï, Bétaré-Oya), in Ngaoundal and as far as the Central African Republic.
Marriage within the group, between Muslims, is preferred; formerly mostly women, today both sexes marry outside.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Mbéré are indigenous: as the first inhabitants of the area, they gave their name to the division.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Society distinguishes the belaka, the djaoro and the baju.
The leaders of the Mbéré association and the chief make the decisions.
Women do not show themselves in front of men, a strictness reinforced by Islam; deference is very marked.
Succession follows Islamic rules, from father to son.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband. People marry around 18-20 years old.
The young man finds out about the family and makes his request with salt; after acceptance, he offers a wrapper and sugar, then a bride price of his choosing.
Formerly, the son-in-law worked for his in-laws; Islam asks only for the bride price (money, bed, suitcase).

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Formerly, a ritual was held at the Belel rock, every two, five or ten years; it disappeared with Islam.
Places of memory: Magowena, Hoka.
Birth is seen as a reincarnation.
Taboos: incest; in her in-laws' home, the wife does not eat chicken.
Divination exists but is receding before Islam.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, livestock rearing (goats, sheep), honey production, in which the Mbéré are experts, fishing. Women: farming and livestock rearing.
To gain access to land, one saw the chief; today, the administration.
Crafts: beehives, pottery (clay pots), mbouillé and mmadam drums.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: The Mbéré are renowned healers, notably for hernias, mental disorders, haemorrhoids and headaches.
Beauty: conduct, height, body; for women, plumpness and conduct.
Courtship: the man shows his capacity for work, a pledge that he will be able to support his family; the woman relies on her figure.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms and dances: mbouillé and ndja'a, on the balafon and the tam-tam, for the millet harvest festival and weddings.
No particular community festival.

sections.title: The names
items: The name takes into account the day and time of birth.
Formerly, a big feast was held and an ox was slaughtered to name the child.
Parents' names are kept; people are honoured and addressed formally by “dressing” their name.

lessons.title: Who are the Mbéré? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Mbéré community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition

vocabulary.frenchText: The father of the lion King's Mountain
The grasses that did not burn

lessons.competence: Introduce the Mbéré community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Mbéré community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Mbéré community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Mbéré community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Mbéré call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Minority group, relatively isolated, in contact with the Bororo and the Fulani; mostly Fulfulde is spoken. • Mbéré is also spoken in the East (Bertoua, Garoua-Boulaï, Bétaré-Oya), at Ngaoundal and as far as the Central African Republic. • Marriage within the group, between Muslims, is preferred; formerly mainly women, today both sexes marry outside. • The Mbéré are indigenous: first inhabitants of the area, they gave their name to the division.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The first occupants of the department that bears their name, the Mbéré live in small numbers among the Bororo and the Fulani, whose language they mostly speak. Strongly Islamised, they are renowned as masters of honey and as healers; farming, goat and sheep rearing and pottery complete their activities.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Mbéré community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Mbéré
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Mbéré organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Mbéré village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Mbéré organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Mbéré village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The society distinguishes the belaka, the djaoro and the baju. • The leaders of the Mbéré association and the chief make the decisions. • Women do not show themselves in front of men, a strictness reinforced by Islam; deference is very marked. • Succession follows Islamic rules, from father to son.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Society distinguishes the belaka, the djaoro and the baju. The leaders of the Mbéré association and the chief make the decisions. Women do not show themselves before men, a strictness reinforced by Islam; deference is very marked.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Mbéré, then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Mbéré
objectives: Linking food to the living environment

vocabulary.langText: bière de mil et de miel

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Mbéré, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Mbéré.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Mbéré, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Mbéré.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: adoka (staple vegetable, also medicinal). • Drinks: afu (millet and honey beer), kpata. • Men: farming, livestock rearing (goats, sheep), honey production, in which the Mbéré are experts, fishing. Women: farming and livestock rearing.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Mbéré mainly eat a staple vegetable, also medicinal. Traditional drinks: millet and honey beer, kpata. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Mbéré: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Mbéré
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Mbéré welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Mbéré family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Mbéré welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Mbéré family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The name takes into account the day and time of birth. • In the past, a great feast was held and an ox slaughtered to name the child. • Parents' names are kept; people are honoured and addressed formally by “dressing” their name. • Birth is seen as a reincarnation. • Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband. People marry at around 18-20.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The name takes into account the day and time of birth. Formerly, a big feast was held and an ox was slaughtered to name the child. Parents' names are kept; people are honoured and addressed formally by “dressing up” their name.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Explain the meaning of three Mbéré personal names and describe the moment when a child receives its name.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

objectives: Putting the stages of marriage in order

lessons.situation: Your elder brother wants to marry a young Mbéré woman. What steps will he have to follow?

steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The young man finds out about the family and makes his request with salt; after acceptance, he offers a wrapper and sugar, then a bride price of his choosing. Formerly, the son-in-law worked for his in-laws; Islam requires only the bride price (money, bed, suitcase).

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Mbéré
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Mbéré, choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Mbéré dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Mbéré, choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.instruction: Among the Mbéré, traditional dances (harvests, weddings, ndja'a) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: balafon, drum, mmadam drum. Festival(s): millet harvest festival.

lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Mbéré
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Mbéré, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Mbéré. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Mbéré, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Mbéré. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, livestock (goats, sheep), honey production, in which the Mbéré are experts, fishing. Women: farming and livestock. • To gain access to land, one used to see the chief; today, the administration. • Crafts: beehives, pottery (canaris), mbouillé and mmadam drums.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, livestock rearing (goats, sheep), honey production, in which the Mbéré are experts, fishing. Women: farming and livestock rearing. To gain access to land, one used to see the chief; today, the administration.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Mbéré's activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Mbéré
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: poulet pour l'épouse dans sa belle-famille

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mbéré, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Mbéré. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mbéré, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Mbéré. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • Formerly, a ritual was held at the Belel rock, every two, five or ten years; it disappeared with Islam. • Places of memory: Magowena, Hoka. • Birth is seen as a reincarnation. • Taboos: incest; in her in-laws' home, the wife does not eat chicken. • Divination exists but is receding before Islam.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Formerly, a ritual was held at the Belel rock, every two, five or ten years; it disappeared with Islam. Places of memory: Magowena, Hoka.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Mbéré (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Mbéré
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Mbéré and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Mbéré family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Mbéré greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Mbéré family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Mbéré. • Greetings: mebafewa = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); nabelakelé = morning greeting (one person); wenobelavelé = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Song, Doh, Mokon, Nyiang, Ndipi. • Parents' names are kept; people are honoured and addressed formally by “dressing” their name.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Mbéré are the first steps towards communicating with the Mbéré. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Mbéré.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Mbéré are the first steps towards communicating with the Mbéré. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
